problem_motivation.content: There is a need for oxygen-resistant refractory high-entropy alloys suitable for high-temperature, high-stress applications.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Oxidation resistance is achieved by silicide coating via pack cementation. A small‐size lattice‐core sandwich is fabricated and tested with high‐temperature flames to demonstrate the versatility of this sequential approach (printing, sintering, and siliconizing) for high‐temperature, high‐stress applications of refractory high‐entropy alloys.

prior_approach.content: The paper cites the use of 3D ink-extrusion printing, interdiffusion, and silicide coating as the method used to synthesize the alloy.
prior_approach.evidence_span: An oxygen‐resistant refractory high‐entropy alloy is synthesized in microlattice or bulk form by 3D ink‐extrusion printing, interdiffusion, and silicide coating.

prior_approach.content: Previous work used silicide coatings for other RHEAs (MoNbTaW, MoNbTaVW, AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr) to form dense SiO2-rich scales.
prior_approach.evidence_span: they have been used to coat MoNbTaW, [ [29] ] MoNbTaVW, [ [30] ] and AlMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr [ [31] ]

prior_approach.content: Zhao et al. previously used 3D ink-extrusion printing to fabricate NbTaTiZr scaffolds.
prior_approach.evidence_span: We are not aware of any published work on 3D ink‐extrusion printing of RHEA, except for Zhao et al. who used 3D ink‐extrusion printing to fabricate equiatomic NbTaTiZr scaffolds

prior_approach.content: The halide-activated pack cementation process for depositing a silicide coating followed a previously published method.
The rheological properties of the ink system have been previously studied in detail.
prior_approach.evidence_span: the rheological properties of the PS‐DBP‐DCM ink system have been studied in detail in Ref. [ [64] ]

prior_limitation.content: LMD is limited by low feature resolution and lack of complex part demonstration.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD.

prior_limitation.content: LPBF is limited by cracking caused by significant thermal stresses from fast cooling.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, cracking usually occurs from significant thermal stresses caused by the very fast cooling rate during the solidification of the melt pool.

prior_limitation.content: The poor oxygen resistance of HfNbTaTiZr prevents its practical high-temperature applications.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, the poor oxygen resistance of HfNbTaTiZr prevents most practical applications at high temperatures.

prior_limitation.content: Prior researchers attribute residual alpha-HCP phases in sintered samples to dissolved oxygen accumulating during sintering, which raises the transition temperature.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: They attribute it to dissolved oxygen accumulated during sintering, which increases the α‐to‐β transition temperature as oxygen is an α‐HCP stabilizer.

mechanism_principle.content: The high yield strength is attributed to interstitial strengthening from oxygen and carbon.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: consistent with the interstitial strengthening of oxygen (≈1.0 wt.%)

mechanism_principle.content: The superior oxidation resistance is explained by the self-healing mechanism where Zr and Hf oxides fill cracks and expel Si.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This is explained by the formation of (Zr,Hf)O 2 filling cracks within the silicide layer and protecting the underlying alloy by expelling Si under the cracks.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors hypothesize that HfNbTaTiZr can be successfully 3D ink-extrusion printed using inks containing blends of metallic and hydride powders.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: In this research, we demonstrate that HfNbTaTiZr can be 3D ink‐extrusion printed from inks containing a blend of metallic and hydride powders.

evidence_result.content: Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy was synthesized.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is synthesized

evidence_result.content: Slow cooling resulted in the formation of both α-HCP and β-BCC phases, while quenching resulted in a metastable single β-BCC phase.
evidence_result.evidence_span: on slow cooling, both α‐HCP and β‐BCC phases are formed, but on quenching, a metastable single β‐BCC phase is obtained.

evidence_result.content: Printed and sintered alloys containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen exhibited excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Printed and sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloys with ≈1 wt.% O shows excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures.

evidence_result.content: The silicide-coated sample shows a parabolic rate constant approximately 700 times lower than the uncoated sample.
evidence_result.evidence_span: parabolic rate constants can be determined for the uncoated sample ( k = 570 mg 2 cm −4 h −1 ), which is ≈700 times higher than that of silicide‐coated sample ( k = 0.80 mg 2 cm −4 h −1 )

constraint.content: The oxygen getter (titanium sponges) was required to be placed in the crucible during sintering to manage oxygen content.
constraint.evidence_span: titanium sponges were placed in the crucible to act as an oxygen getter during sintering

constraint.content: The surface of the sintered samples had to be flat and parallel to ensure uniaxial compression during testing.
constraint.evidence_span: To ensure uniaxial compression, the top and bottom surfaces of sintered samples were ground flat and parallel before the compression test
